blueprints.title: Work out powers
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2⁵ means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times. The small raised number (the power) counts how many 2s there are; it is not a number to multiply by.

screens.title: Count them out
text: Write the number as many times as the power says, with × between them. Then multiply two at a time.

strategies.title: Build it up one step at a time

screens.title: Multiply again and again
text: Start with the number and multiply by it again for each extra power. That is one multiplication fewer than the power.

strategies.title: Use the multiplication facts you know

screens.title: Each step is a fact
text: Every step of a power is a multiplication fact: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. If a step is slow, say that times table first.

blueprints.title: Expand a bracket: a(x + b)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The number outside multiplies everything inside
text: 3(x + 4) means three lots of (x + 4): (x + 4) + (x + 4) + (x + 4). That is three x's and three 4s.
chapter.tip: Multiply every term in the bracket, not only the first one.

screens.title: Split the rectangle
text: Draw a rectangle a high and x + b long. Split the long side into x and b. The two parts have areas a × x and a × b; together they are the whole rectangle.

screens.title: Multiply along each arrow
text: Draw an arrow from the number outside the bracket to each term inside it, and multiply along each arrow.

screens.title: The last term is a fact
text: The number at the end is the number outside times the number inside: 3 × 4 = 12. If that fact is slow, rebuild it from one you know: 3 × 4 is 3 × 2 doubled.

blueprints.title: Expand (x + a)(x + b)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Four products
text: In (x + 2)(x + 5), each term of the first bracket multiplies each term of the second: x × x, x × 5, 2 × x and 2 × 5.
chapter.tip: The x term is the SUM of the two numbers; the last term is their PRODUCT.

screens.title: Fill the four cells
text: Draw a 2 by 2 grid. Write x and a along the top, x and b down the side. Fill each cell with the product of its row and column, then add the two cells that have an x.

screens.title: Two of the four products have an x
text: Multiply the first terms, the outer terms, the inner terms and the last terms. The outer and inner products are the two x terms: add them.

screens.title: Keep each sign
text: When a number is negative, keep its sign in each product. The x term is the sum of the two signed products, so a negative product makes it smaller.

strategies.title: (a + b)²: why the middle term is 2ab

screens.title: The idea
text: (a + b)² = (a + b)(a + b). Multiplying every term by every term gives a×a, a×b, b×a and b×b.
a×b and b×a are the same, and there are TWO of them: a² + 2ab + b². The area picture shows them as two equal rectangles.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 20

screens.title: Another example
text: The same idea on a different question.
math: The box is the x coefficient: -48

screens.title: Multiply it out
text: Write (px + q)² as (px + q)(px + q) and multiply each term by each term.
The two middle products come out equal, so the middle term is doubled.

screens.title: Another way: Multiply it out: four products
text: The same answer by another valid method.

screens.title: The middle term is 2ab: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to write the middle term as ab. The identity has 2ab: the two products 5x × 7 and 7 × 5x are both there.
There are two middle products, a×b and b×a; together they make 2ab.
math: Check at x = 1: the left side is 144. With the middle term 70: 25 + 70 + 49 = 144. With 35 instead: 109, which is not 144.

screens.title: The middle term is 2ab: solved correctly
text: Watch the middle term: it is a×b and b×a together, so it is twice the product, 2ab.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 70

strategies.title: The sign of the middle term

screens.title: The sign of the middle term: a common mix-up
text: The middle term of (a + b)² is +2ab.
Square of a sum: +2ab. Square of a difference: −2ab.
math: Check at x = 1: the left side is 81. With the middle term 40: 25 + 40 + 16 = 81. With -40 instead: 1, which is not 81.

screens.title: The sign of the middle term: solved correctly
text: Watch the sign of the middle term: with a plus inside the bracket, all three terms are added.
math: The box is the x coefficient: 40

blueprints.title: Differentiate powers of x
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The power rule
text: To differentiate k xⁿ, bring the power down as a factor and lower the power by one: the derivative is k n xⁿ⁻¹. Then put in the value of x.
chapter.tip: Lower the power first, then substitute.

strategies.title: A derivative is a rate of change

screens.title: Not the value: how fast it changes
text: f′(3) is how fast f is changing at x = 3, not the value f(3). For f(x) = x², the values at 2.9, 3 and 3.1 are 8.41, 9 and 9.61: they rise by 1.2 over 0.2, which is 6 per unit, and the rule gives 2 × 3 = 6.

screens.title: In this order
text: Multiply the coefficient by the power, then take one off the power. Only then put in the number.

screens.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2² = 2 × 2 = 4 and 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A power is not the number times the power: 2³ is not 6.

blueprints.title: Integrate powers of x
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Reverse the power rule
text: Differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) gives xⁿ. So an antiderivative of k xⁿ is k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1): raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.
math: ∫ k xⁿ dx = k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) + C

chapter.title: Between two limits
text: For a definite integral, work out the antiderivative F at the upper limit and at the lower limit, then subtract: F(upper) − F(lower). The constant C cancels.

screens.title: Undo, then check
text: Whatever antiderivative you write, differentiate it: you must get back the function you started with. x³ differentiates to 3x², so ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

screens.title: Two moves, then the limits
text: Add one to the power, then divide by that new power. Then put in the upper limit and the lower limit, and subtract.

screens.title: What the working needs
text: The working needs powers (2³ = 8) and fractions with the same denominator (16⁄3 − 2⁄3 = 14⁄3). If either is slow, practise it first; the integration itself is two moves.

blueprints.title: Integrate by substitution
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Spot u and du
text: In ∫ 2x(x² + 1)² dx, call the inside of the bracket u = x² + 1. Its derivative, 2x, is already there: du = 2x dx. So the integral is ∫ u² du.

chapter.title: Change the limits
text: With limits, change them too: put each x limit into u = x² + 1, and integrate between those u values. You never go back to x.
chapter.tip: Using the x limits for u is the most common slip.

screens.title: Nothing left to divide by
text: du ⁄ dx = 2x, so a small change dx in x changes u by 2x dx. The 2x in the integral is exactly what turns dx into du: there is no extra 2 to divide by.

strategies.title: Make a little table of limits

screens.title: x row, u row
text: Write two rows, x and u. Under x put the two limits; under u put x² + c for each. Then integrate in u between the u values.

screens.title: The last step is arithmetic
text: The last step is powers of whole numbers, like 2³ = 8 and 5³ = 125, then a subtraction and a division. A power is repeated multiplication, not the number times the power.

blueprints.title: How many solutions? The discriminant
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: b² − 4ac decides
text: For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac. Positive: two different real solutions. Zero: one (repeated) solution. Negative: no real solutions.
chapter.tip: b² is never negative, even when b is.

screens.title: Crossings
text: y = x² + bx + c is a U-shaped curve. Two solutions: it crosses the x-axis twice. One: it just touches it. None: it stays above it. The discriminant tells you which, without drawing.

strategies.title: Write each part with its sign

screens.title: b², then 4ac, then subtract
text: Write b², then 4ac with c's own sign, then subtract.

screens.title: Two sign facts
text: Taking away a negative number adds: 16 − (−20) = 36. And a square is never negative: (−4)² = 16.

blueprints.title: Solving a linear inequality
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Like an equation, with one extra rule
text: Solve a linear inequality as you would an equation. But when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign reverses: < becomes > and > becomes <.
math: Divide by −6 (negative, so the sign flips): x > 0

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve 5x − 6 < 14. Write the answer as an inequality for x (e.g. x > 2).” A common wrong answer is x ≤ 4.
The boundary value was included; with < it is not part of the answer.

screens.title: Multiplying by a negative reverses the order
text: 3 < 5, but −3 > −5: multiplying by a negative number reverses the order of numbers on the number line. So whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the sign. Dividing by a positive number keeps it.

screens.title: Get x alone, watching signs
text: Move the constant to the other side. Then divide by the coefficient of x; if that coefficient is negative, reverse the sign. Write the answer as x > k or x < k.

screens.title: Pick a number from your answer
text: If your answer is x > 0, try x = 1 in the original inequality. If it makes the inequality true, and a number on the other side makes it false, the answer is likely correct. If not, check the sign flip.

blueprints.title: Collecting like terms
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Like terms have the same letter part
text: 3x and −5x are like terms because both have x. 3x and 2y are not like terms. Add or subtract like terms by combining their numbers; leave unlike terms separate.
chapter.tip: Keep the sign with the term that follows it. −9y means the sign − belongs to 9y.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Simplify 9x − 9y − 5x − 3y.” A common wrong answer is −8xy.
x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.

screens.title: Rewrite with like terms together
text: Rearrange so all the x terms are together and all the y terms are together. Keep each sign attached to its term. Then add the numbers in front of each group.

screens.title: Cannot add apples and oranges
text: 3x + 2y cannot be simplified further: x and y are different unknowns. Only terms with exactly the same letter part can combine. x² and x are also unlike terms.

screens.title: Same sign: add and keep. Different sign: subtract and keep the bigger one's sign.
text: −9 + (−7) = −16 (same sign: add, keep negative). 5 + (−3) = 2 (different sign: 5 − 3, keep positive). If adding signed numbers is slow, practise integer addition first.

blueprints.title: The derivative from first principles
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The slope of the tangent
text: f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h: the slope of the chord from x to x + h as the second point slides towards the first.
Simplify f(x + h) − f(x) until h is a factor of the top, cancel h, then let h → 0.
math: f(x + h) − f(x) = 2xh + h² − 5h = h(2x + h − 5)
Divide by h: 2x + h − 5; let h → 0: f′(x) = 2x − 5

chapter.title: A fraction: one common denominator
text: For a fraction, write f(x + h) − f(x) over one common denominator: the top becomes a multiple of h, which cancels.

chapter.title: A square root: multiply by the sum of the roots
text: For a square root, multiply top and bottom by the sum of the two roots. The top becomes (x + h + 2) − (x + 2) = h, which cancels.
math: So the chord slope is 1 ⁄ [√(x + h + 2) + √(x + 2)]

chapter.title: Sine and cosine: the two special limits
text: Expand with the compound-angle formula, then use the two limits (sin 2h)/h → 2 and (cos 2h − 1)/h → 0 as h → 0.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Using the definition f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, find f′(x) for f(x) = 2x² + 4x − 1.” A common wrong answer is 4x + 3.
The constant −1 was kept; in f(x + h) − f(x) it cancels, so it does not appear in f′(x).

screens.title: Three stages
text: Stage one: write f(x + h) and simplify f(x + h) − f(x) until every term of the top has a factor h: expand a polynomial, combine fractions, or multiply by the sum of the roots. Stage two: cancel h. Stage three: let h → 0.

screens.title: A chord is not a tangent
text: With h equal to zero straight away, the fraction is zero over zero: it has no value. The limit lets h shrink towards zero without reaching it. Cancelling h first removes the zero over zero and shows the value the chord slopes approach.

screens.title: Do not lose the cross terms
text: (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², not x² + h². (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B. A missing middle term loses the answer.

blueprints.title: Degrees to radians
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: π radians = 180°
text: One radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius. A half turn is exactly π radians, so multiply an angle in degrees by π/180 and simplify the fraction.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Convert −690° into radians. Write the answer in terms of π (you may type pi).” A common wrong answer is −23π/12.
A full turn was taken as π radians; a full turn is 2π radians, and π is a half turn (180°).

screens.title: One formula
text: Radians = degrees × π/180. Simplify the fraction by dividing the top and bottom by their highest common factor; keep a minus sign for a negative angle.

screens.title: Landmark angles
text: Learn these landmarks. Any angle that is a multiple of one of them converts by scaling it.

screens.title: Highest common factor with 180
text: 180 = 4 × 45 = 6 × 30 = 12 × 15. The highest common factor of the angle and 180 tells you how far to simplify: 120/180 = 2/3, so 120° = 2π/3.

blueprints.title: Using sec²θ − tan²θ = 1
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Factorise sec²θ − tan²θ = 1
text: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 is a difference of two squares: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1. So if you know the sum, the difference is its reciprocal.
math: Add: 2 sec θ = 5/2, so sec θ = 5/4
Subtract: 2 tan θ = 3/2, so tan θ = 3/4

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “If sec θ + tan θ = 7/3 for an acute angle θ, find sin θ.” A common wrong answer is 29/20.
The ratio was turned upside down: sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ.

screens.title: Their product is 1
text: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so if sec θ + tan θ = k then sec θ − tan θ = 1/k. The same works for cosec and cot, because cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1.

strategies.title: Add and subtract the two equations

screens.title: Two equations, two unknowns
text: Add the sum and the difference and halve: that is sec θ (or cosec θ). Subtract and halve: that is tan θ (or cot θ). Then sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ, and cos θ = cot θ ÷ cosec θ.

screens.title: Common denominator
text: k + 1/k: write k as k/1, so the common denominator is k: k + 1/k = (k² + 1)/k. Halving gives (k² + 1)/(2k). For k = 7/3: 7/3 + 3/7 = 58/21, and half of it is 29/21.

blueprints.title: Finding a side with the sine rule
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: a/sin A = b/sin B
text: In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of the angle opposite it gives the same number. To find an unknown side, set up the proportion and solve.
math: In triangle ABC: A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 2

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “In triangle ABC, A = 30°, B = 135° and a = 11 cm. Using the sine rule, find b in cm. Give the exact value.” A common wrong answer is 99/2.
The sides were taken in the same ratio as the angles; sides are in the ratio of the SINES of the opposite angles.

screens.title: Match each side to its opposite angle
text: Write a/sin A = b/sin B. Put the known side and its opposite angle on one side, the unknown side and its opposite angle on the other. Multiply across and simplify the surds.

strategies.title: The sine of an obtuse angle

screens.title: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ
text: An obtuse angle has the same sine as its supplement, so sin 135° = sin 45°. Use that value in the proportion exactly as before.

screens.title: sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, sin 90° = 1
text: These values come from the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles. When the question asks for an exact answer, use them rather than a decimal.

blueprints.title: Solving a linear equation with negative numbers
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Negative coefficients and constants
text: When the coefficient of x or the numbers are negative, the method is the same: undo in reverse order. Take care when subtracting a negative (which adds) and when dividing by a negative (which changes the sign of the result).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve −2x + 8 = −2.” A common wrong answer is −3.
8 was moved to the other side without changing its sign: subtracting 8 from −2 gives −10.

strategies.title: Do the same to both sides

screens.title: Add or subtract, then divide
text: Add or subtract the number on the x side from both sides so the x term is alone. Then divide both sides by the coefficient of x.

screens.title: Same signs give positive, different signs give negative
text: When dividing (or multiplying), two numbers with the same sign give a positive result and two numbers with different signs give a negative result. This decides the sign of x.

screens.title: Subtracting a negative adds
text: −6 − (−10) = −6 + 10 = 4: taking away a negative number is the same as adding it. And 4 ÷ (−4) = −1: different signs give a negative result. If either is slow, practise integer arithmetic first.

blueprints.title: The domain of a real function
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Where the formula works
text: The domain is every real x for which the formula gives a real number: what is under a square root must not be negative, and a denominator must not be zero.
math: Divide by −6 (negative, so the sign flips): x ≤ 0

chapter.title: A quadratic under the root or below the line
text: Factorise the quadratic and mark its roots. A quadratic with a positive x² term is negative between its roots and positive outside them (with a negative x² term it is the other way round). Under a square root keep where it is ≥ 0, roots included; in a denominator remove the roots; under a square root in a denominator keep where it is > 0, roots excluded.
math: Roots 1 and 2: the quadratic is negative between them and positive outside

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(3x − 2). Write it in interval notation.” A common wrong answer is (2/3, ∞).
x = 2/3 was left out; √0 = 0 is a real number, so the end point belongs to the domain.

strategies.title: Write the condition, then solve it

screens.title: Square root and denominator
text: Under a square root: set the expression ≥ 0. In a denominator: set it ≠ 0. A square root in a denominator: set it > 0. Solve the condition and write the answer in interval notation.

screens.title: A round bracket excludes, a square bracket includes
text: (a, b) means a < x < b and [a, b] means a ≤ x ≤ b. Infinity always takes a round bracket. Two separate pieces are joined with ∪.

screens.title: Flip when dividing by a negative
text: −6x ≥ 0: divide by −6 and reverse the sign, so x ≤ 0. Forgetting the reversal is the most common slip in domain questions. For a quadratic, factorise first and test one number in each region.

blueprints.title: Expressing log N in terms of log 2 and log 3
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Three laws of logarithms
text: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y and log xⁿ = n log x. With log 2 = a and log 3 = b, any number built from 2s, 3s and powers of 10 can be written in a and b.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Given log 2 = a and log 3 = b (logarithms to base 10), express log 51.84 in terms of a and b.” A common wrong answer is 2a + 2b.
log 5 was taken as log 2 + log 3, because 2 + 3 = 5; logs turn products into sums, and 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so log 5 = 1 − a.

screens.title: Factorise, then apply the laws
text: Write N as a product of powers of 2, 3 and 10. Use the product rule (the log of a product is the sum of the logs) and the power rule (the log of a power is the power times the log). Replace log 10 by 1.

screens.title: The log of ten is one
text: The logarithms are to base ten, so the log of ten is one and the log of one is zero. Write five as ten divided by two, and a decimal as a whole number times a power of ten.

screens.title: 0.05 = 5 × 10⁻²
text: A decimal is a whole number times a negative power of ten: 0.06 = 6 × 10⁻², so log 0.06 = log 2 + log 3 − 2. Numbers between 0 and 1 have negative logarithms.

blueprints.title: Exact values by compound-angle formulas
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: sin, cos and tan of A ± B
text: Use the formula for the sum or difference, put in the exact values of each angle, multiply out the surds and simplify.
math: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) ⁄ (1 ∓ tan A tan B)

chapter.title: Angles beyond a right angle, and tan
text: For an angle beyond a right angle, find its reference angle and its sign from its quadrant, then use the formula as before. A tan answer with a root in the denominator is rationalised.
math: tan 30° = 1/√3; 135° is in the second quadrant, reference angle 45°, so tan 135° = −1

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Use a compound-angle formula to find the exact value of cos(60° − 45°). Simplify fully, with no square root in the denominator.” A common wrong answer is (1 − √2)/2.
cos(A − B) was split as cos A − cos B; cos does not distribute over a sum, so use the compound-angle formula.

screens.title: Write each value with its sign
text: Write sin, cos (or tan) of each of the two angles, with the sign from its quadrant. Substitute into the formula, multiply out the surds and simplify; rationalise a tan answer.

screens.title: sin keeps the sign, cos swaps it
text: sin(A + B) has a plus between its two products and sin(A − B) a minus. cos(A + B) has a minus and cos(A − B) a plus: the sign in the cos formula is the opposite of the sign between A and B. In the tan formula the top keeps the sign and the bottom swaps it.

screens.title: √a × √b = √(ab)
text: (1/2)(√2/2) = √2/4: multiply tops and multiply bottoms. √2 × √3 = √6. With a common denominator the terms add: √2/4 + √6/4 = (√2 + √6)/4.

blueprints.title: Where a function is increasing or decreasing
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: f′(x) > 0 means increasing
text: A function is strictly increasing where its derivative is positive and strictly decreasing where its derivative is negative. Find f′(x), find where it is zero, then decide its sign between those points.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the interval(s) on which f(x) = −2x³ − 12x² − 1 is strictly decreasing. Write open intervals, joined by ∪ if there are two (for example (−∞, p) ∪ (q, ∞)).” A common wrong answer is (−4, 0).
The negative leading coefficient was ignored: f′ opens downwards, so it is positive between the roots and negative outside them.

screens.title: Roots of f′, then test the intervals
text: The roots of f′(x) = 0 divide the number line into intervals. Test one x in each interval: where f′(x) > 0, f is increasing; where f′(x) < 0, f is decreasing. Write open intervals.

strategies.title: Why the sign of f′ matters

screens.title: Uphill and downhill
text: f′(x) is the slope of the tangent. A positive slope means the graph goes uphill (increasing); a negative slope means downhill (decreasing). Where the slope is zero the graph turns.

screens.title: Take out the common factor first
text: −6x² − 42x − 72: take out −6 to get −6(x² + 7x + 12), then factorise: −6(x + 3)(x + 4). The roots are x = −3 and x = −4. The factor −6 is negative, so it flips the sign of the bracket product.

blueprints.title: Separating the variables
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Put y on one side, x on the other
text: When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, separate the variables: everything with y (and dy) on one side, everything with x (and dx) on the other. Integrate both sides and use the starting value to find the constant.
math: y = 1 when x = 0 gives C = 0, so y = e^(−2x² − 3x)

chapter.title: When dy/dx is a number times y/x
text: Separating gives ln|y| = k ln x + C, so y is a power of x: y = A xᵏ. The starting value gives A.
math: ln|y| = 3 ln x + C, so y = A x³
y = 2 when x = 1 gives A = 2: y = 2x³

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve the differential equation dy/dx = (−3x − 1)y, given that y = 2 when x = 0. Write y in terms of x.” A common wrong answer is −3x²/2 − x + 2.
The y on the right was ignored and only (px + q) was integrated; divide by y first: dy/y = (px + q) dx.

screens.title: In order
text: Rewrite with y and dy on one side and x and dx on the other. Integrate both sides, adding one constant. Use the starting value to find the constant, then write y on its own.

screens.title: Each side has one variable
text: After separating, one side depends only on y and the other only on x, so each can be integrated on its own. The two constants of integration combine into one.

chapter.title: 0 ⁄ 0 does not mean the limit is 0

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find lim (x → 6) of (x² − 36) ⁄ (x − 6).” A common wrong answer is 0.

strategies.title: Spot the difference of two squares

screens.title: x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a)
text: The top is k(x² − a²) = k(x − a)(x + a). The bottom, x − a, cancels with one factor, leaving k(x + a). Putting x = a then gives k(a + a).

screens.title: The order matters
text: Putting the number in straight away gives nothing useful. Cancel the factor that makes both top and bottom zero; only then put the number in: the simplified expression has a value there.

screens.title: Expand the brackets back
text: (x − 3)(x + 3) = x² + 3x − 3x − 9 = x² − 9. If expanding does not give what you started with, the factorisation is wrong. A difference of two squares always has this shape.

blueprints.title: Solving a trigonometric equation in [0, 2π)
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: One reference angle, several solutions
text: Get the ratio on its own, then find the reference angle α: the acute angle whose ratio is the value without its sign. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, so the solutions are α and π − α.
math: sin x = 1/√2: the reference angle is π/4
sin is positive in quadrants I and II: x = π/4 or x = π − π/4 = 3π/4

chapter.title: Multiple angles: sin kx, cos kx, tan kx
text: When the angle is 2x and 0 ≤ x < 2π, the angle 2x goes round twice: 0 ≤ 2x < 4π. Solve for the angle 2x in the first turn, add 2π to each solution for the second turn, then divide every value by 2. For 3x there are three turns, so add 2π twice.
math: sin 2x = 1/2: the reference angle is π/6; sin is positive in I and II

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve 2 sin x − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π (x in radians). Give every solution in radians, in terms of π, separated by commas (type π or pi): for example π/4, 3π/2 (and 0 for x = 0).” A common wrong answer is π/6.
Only the principal value was given; sin takes each value twice in every 2π, so look in every quadrant where it has this sign.

screens.title: All, Sin, Tan, Cos
text: In the first quadrant all three ratios are positive; in the second only sine; in the third only tangent; in the fourth only cosine. The angles with reference angle α are α, π − α, π + α and 2π − α: keep the ones in quadrants where the ratio has the sign you need.

For a negative value, take the reference angle of the value without its sign and keep the quadrants where the ratio is negative. When the value is zero, one or minus one, the angle lies on an axis: read it from the unit circle.

strategies.title: Reference angle, place it, then every turn

screens.title: The whole method
text: Rearrange so the ratio of the angle stands alone. Find the reference angle and place it in the quadrants with the right sign: these are the values of the angle in the first turn. If the angle is kx, add 2π to each value, again and again, until the angle reaches 2kπ. Divide every value by k.

screens.title: Convert if needed
text: The question asks for radians: π is 180°, so π/6 = 30°, π/4 = 45°, π/3 = 60°. If you work in degrees first, convert each answer at the end by dividing by 180 and writing π.

math: Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 55°. What is the other angle, in degrees?

screens.title: Supplement of an obtuse angle

strategies.title: Adjacent angles on a straight line

screens.title: Larger adjacent angle

Map to real: multiply the map length by the scale. The real distance is the bigger number.
math: On a map, 1 cm stands for 50 km. Two villages are 10 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they really, in km?
10 cm × 50 km for each cm = 500 km

strategies.title: From the real distance to the map

screens.title: From the real distance to the map
text: The map is smaller than the real world, so the map distance is the smaller number.
Real to map: divide the real distance by the scale.
math: On a map, 1 cm stands for 2 km. Two towns are really 26 km apart. How far apart are they on the map, in cm?
26 km ÷ 2 km for each cm = 13 cm

strategies.title: A plan scale written as a ratio

screens.title: A plan scale written as a ratio
text: A scale of one to n means every real length is n times the length on the plan, in the same unit.
Multiply the plan length by n to get real centimetres, then divide by a hundred to get metres.
math: A plan is drawn to the scale 1 : 500. A wall is 19 cm long on the plan. How long is the real wall, in metres?
Every 1 cm stands for 500 cm: 19 × 500 = 9500 cm

strategies.title: A map scale written as a ratio

screens.title: A map scale written as a ratio
text: A scale of one to n means every real length is n times the length on the map, in the same unit.
Multiply the map length by n to get real centimetres, then divide by a hundred thousand to get kilometres.
math: A map is drawn to the scale 1 : 25000. A road is 14 cm long on the map. How long is the real road, in km?
Every 1 cm stands for 25000 cm: 14 × 25000 = 350000 cm

blueprints.title: Missing numbers and related facts
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Missing numbers and related facts
text: Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing. To find a missing number, ask what was done to it, then work backwards; put your answer back in to check.

strategies.title: A number was added to the box

screens.title: A number was added to the box
text: Ask what was done to the box: a number was added to it, and the total is on the other side.
Undo the adding: take that number away from the total. Then put your answer in the box and check that the sentence is true.
math: 10 was added to the box: undo it by taking 10 away

strategies.title: The box is the number taken away

screens.title: The box is the number taken away
text: Here the box is taken away from the first number, and the number on the right is what is left.
So the box is the first number take away what is left. Check by taking your answer away from the first number.
math: The box was taken away from 20 and 6 is left, so the box is 20 − 6

strategies.title: A number was taken away from the box

screens.title: A number was taken away from the box
text: A number was taken away from the box, and the number on the right is what is left.
Undo the taking away: add that number back to what is left. Check by taking it away again.
math: 3 was taken away from the box: undo it by adding 3 back

screens.title: The box was multiplied
text: The box was multiplied by a number, and the product is on the other side.
Undo the multiplying: divide the product by that number, using the times table. Check by multiplying.
math: The box was multiplied by 7: undo it by dividing by 7

strategies.title: The subtraction fact of an addition

screens.title: The subtraction fact of an addition
text: An addition fact and its subtraction facts are one family: a total and its two parts.
A subtraction fact starts with the total and takes away one part; what is left is the other part.
math: 6,712 + 4,470 = 11,182. Which subtraction fact belongs to the same fact family?

screens.title: Check a subtraction by adding
text: Adding undoes taking away.
To check a subtraction, add the answer to the number taken away: you should get the number you started with.
math: Priya worked out 5,449 − 425 = 5,024. Which addition can Priya use to check this answer?

strategies.title: The division fact of a multiplication

screens.title: The division fact of a multiplication
text: Multiplying and dividing undo each other: a product and its two factors are one family.
A division fact starts with the product and divides it by one factor; the answer is the other factor.
math: 11 × 12 = 132. Which division fact comes from this multiplication fact?

screens.title: Dividend = divisor × quotient
text: In a division the dividend is the number being divided, the divisor divides it and the quotient is the answer.
Multiplying undoes dividing, so the dividend equals the divisor times the quotient.
math: In 110 ÷ 10 = 11, 110 is the dividend, 10 the divisor and 11 the quotient. Which sentence shows dividend = divisor × quotient for it?
Check: 10 × 11 = 110, so the sentence is true

screens.title: Not both numbers added: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add both numbers you can see. Adding them never undoes what was done to the box.
Ask what was done to the box, then undo it: the missing number is found by taking away, not by adding the two numbers.

screens.title: Not both numbers added: solved correctly
text: Ask what number added to the given one makes the total: take it away from the total to find the box; do not add the two numbers.
math: 2 was added to the box: undo it by taking 2 away

screens.title: Not both numbers added: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add both numbers you can see. Adding them never undoes what was done to the box.
Ask what was done to the box, then undo it: the missing number is found by taking away, not by adding the two numbers.

screens.title: Not both numbers added: solved correctly
text: Ask what number taken from the first one leaves the second: take the second away from the first to find the box; do not add the two numbers.
math: The box was taken away from 18 and 3 is left, so the box is 18 − 3

strategies.title: Add it back, do not take it away again

screens.title: Add it back, do not take it away again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take the number away a second time.
The box is the number before anything was taken away, so add the number back to what is left.

screens.title: Add it back, do not take it away again: solved correctly
text: The box had a number taken away from it, so add that number back on to find it; do not take it away again.
math: 7 was taken away from the box: undo it by adding 7 back

blueprints.title: Solving a one-step equation
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Solving a one-step equation
text: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone; put your answer back in to check.

strategies.title: A number is added to x

screens.title: A number is added to x
text: A number is added to x.
Take that number away from both sides, so x is alone. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

strategies.title: A number is taken away from x

screens.title: A number is taken away from x
text: A number is taken away from x.
Add that number to both sides, so x is alone. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

strategies.title: x is multiplied by a number

screens.title: x is multiplied by a number
text: The number written next to x multiplies it.
Divide both sides by that number, so x is alone. Check by multiplying.

strategies.title: x is divided by a number

screens.title: x is divided by a number
text: x is divided by a number.
Multiply both sides by that number, so x is alone. Check by dividing.

strategies.title: Do the opposite, not the same again

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to do the same operation again instead of its opposite.
To leave x alone, undo what was done to x: take away a number that was added, add back a number that was taken away, divide by a number that multiplies x, multiply by a number that divides x.

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: solved correctly
text: Undo adding by taking away the same number from both sides, not by adding it again.

strategies.title: Do the opposite, not the same again

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to do the same operation again instead of its opposite.
To leave x alone, undo what was done to x: take away a number that was added, add back a number that was taken away, divide by a number that multiplies x, multiply by a number that divides x.

screens.title: Do the opposite, not the same again: solved correctly
text: Undo taking away by adding the number back to both sides, not by taking it away again.

strategies.title: Divide by the number next to x

screens.title: Divide by the number next to x: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to take away the number next to x.
That number multiplies x, so undo it by dividing both sides by it.

screens.title: Divide by the number next to x: solved correctly
text: The number next to x multiplies it, so divide both sides by that number; do not take it away.

screens.title: Multiply, do not add: a common mix-up
text: A common mix-up is to add the number instead of multiplying by it.
x was divided by the number, so undo it by multiplying both sides by it.

screens.title: Multiply, do not add: solved correctly
text: x was divided by the number, so multiply both sides by it; do not add it.

blueprints.title: Finding a missing digit by undoing
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Finding a missing digit by undoing
text: A sum or difference is a true sentence. When the hidden digit is in the first number, undo the operation to find the whole first number, then read the digit.

strategies.title: A digit hidden in a number being added

screens.title: A digit hidden in a number being added
text: The two numbers being added make the total, so the number with the hidden digit is a part.
A missing part is the total take away the other part. Work that out, read the digit in the box's place, and check by doing the whole addition.
math: The first number is the total take away the other part: 713 − 255 = 458

strategies.title: A digit hidden in the first number of a subtraction

screens.title: A digit hidden in the first number of a subtraction
text: The first number of a subtraction is what you started with.
Undo the taking away: add the answer to the number taken away, read the digit in the box's place, and check by doing the subtraction.
math: The first number is the answer add the number taken away: 218 + 168 = 386

blueprints.title: The nth term of a geometric progression
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Multiply by the same number each time
text: In a geometric progression each term is the one before multiplied by the common ratio r. Find r by dividing the second term by the first. From the first term to the nth term there is one multiplication fewer than the term number, so the nth term is a times r to that power.

chapter.title: A negative ratio
text: When the ratio is negative the terms alternate in sign. Keep brackets round the negative ratio when you raise it to a power: an even power of a negative number is positive, an odd power is negative.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the 8th term of the geometric progression −3, 9, −27, …” A common wrong answer is 81.
The common difference was used as in an AP; each term here is −3 times the one before.

screens.title: In order
text: Divide the second term by the first to get r. Raise r to the power one less than the term number. Multiply by the first term. Watch the sign when r is negative.

screens.title: One fewer than the term number
text: From the first term to the second is one multiplication by r, to the third is two. So the nth term is one fewer than n multiplications away from the first term. Using n multiplications gives the term after it.

screens.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, not 2 × 4 = 8. (−3)³ = −27 and (−3)⁴ = 81: brackets keep the minus sign inside the power.

blueprints.title: Choosing k to make a function continuous
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: The two pieces must meet
text: f is continuous at the joining point when the left piece and the right piece give the same value there. Put the joining value of x into both pieces, set them equal and solve for k.
math: Left piece at x = 1: k × 1 + 1 = k + 1

chapter.title: A gap at the point: k is the limit
text: When the formula gives 0 ⁄ 0 at the point, f is continuous exactly when k equals the limit of the formula there. Use the standard limits, or rationalise a square root.
math: 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), so (1 − cos θ)/θ² → 1/2
(√(1 + mx) − 1)/x = m ⁄ (√(1 + mx) + 1) → m/2 (multiply top and bottom by √(1 + mx) + 1)

chapter.title: A cube over a linear factor
text: Factorise the difference of two cubes, a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), cancel the common factor, then substitute.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “f(x) = sin(x)/(3x) for x ≠ 0, and f(0) = k. Find the value of k for which f is continuous at x = 0.” A common wrong answer is 3.
The ratio was turned over, giving 3: the number in the sine goes on top, since sin(x)/(3x) = (1/3) × sin(x)/x, which tends to 1/3.

screens.title: Set them equal, solve for k
text: Write the value the function approaches at the point (from each piece, or the limit of the formula) and the value at the point. Set them equal and solve for k.

screens.title: No jump and no gap
text: Continuous at a point means you can draw the graph through it without lifting your pen: the value approached from the left, the value approached from the right and the value at the point are the same number.

screens.title: Three standard results
text: sin θ / θ → 1 as θ → 0. 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), so (1 − cos θ)/θ² → 1/2. (√(1 + θ) − 1)/θ → 1/2, found by multiplying top and bottom by √(1 + θ) + 1. Scale each one for sin(mx), cos(mx) or √(1 + mx).

blueprints.title: Trigonometric functions of any angle
blueprints.author: OpenPath (written with AI assistance; not educator-reviewed)

chapter.title: Reference angle and quadrant sign
text: Bring the angle into one turn by adding or taking away whole turns. Its reference angle is its distance from the nearest part of the x-axis. The value is the reference angle's value with the sign of the function in that quadrant (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).
math: 120° is in the second quadrant: reference angle 180° − 120° = 60°
cos is negative in the second quadrant

chapter.title: Negative or large angles, and cosec, sec, cot
text: Add or take away whole turns to bring the angle into one turn. cosec, sec and cot are the reciprocals of sin, cos and tan: find sin, cos or tan first, then take the reciprocal and rationalise.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the exact value of sec 840°. Simplify fully, with no square root in the denominator.” A common wrong answer is 2.
The sign was wrong: in the quadrant of 840°, sec is negative.

screens.title: In order
text: Add or take away whole turns. Find the quadrant and the reference angle. Write the value of the reference angle, then give it the sign of the function in that quadrant. For cosec, sec or cot take the reciprocal.

screens.title: All, Sin, Tan, Cos
text: In the first quadrant all the functions are positive; in the second only sin and cosec; in the third only tan and cot; in the fourth only cos and sec. The reference angle is the angle to the x-axis.

screens.title: sin, cos and tan of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°
text: sin: 0, 1/2, √2/2, √3/2, 1. cos: 1, √3/2, √2/2, 1/2, 0. tan: 0, 1/√3, 1, √3, and undefined at 90°. They come from half a square and half an equilateral triangle.
